title: Python parsing under a contract
summary: Turn a CSV delivery and a JSON delivery from two fictional plants into typed Python values under one small contract, or reject each record with a named reason and its raw input, so that accepted plus rejected equals received; a third plant's transfer delivery breaks the same rules in new ways.
outcome: Parse and validate records with explicit types, tell null from missing from blank from zero, keep rejections with reasons, log without side effects at import, and prove each rule with a test that fails for the stated defect.
environment: Python 3.12 standard library only; nothing to install.
evidence: 36 tests executed locally with zero skips; a shipped mutation check shows fourteen one-line defects each failing a test. Hashes in docs/academy/labs/lab-l01-python-parsing.json.
downloadDescription: Parsing lab: CSV and JSON deliveries, a transfer delivery, authored expected results, a naive and a starter parser, a reference solution, tests and a mutation check. Python 3.12 standard library.

title: SQL and PySpark equivalence
summary: The same typed synthetic inspection data transformed with Spark SQL and with the DataFrame API; results and types are compared deliberately, including an order-dependent failure and null-handling divergences until corrected.
outcome: Write the same transformation both ways, compare schemas and sorted rows, and explain why implicit row order and null comparisons break equivalence.
environment: Python 3.12, Apache Spark 4.0.4 (PySpark, local[2], UI off), Java 21.
evidence: 9 tests executed locally with zero skips; fixture and output hashes in docs/academy/labs/lab-l02-sql-pyspark-equivalence.json.
downloadDescription: Equivalence lab: fixtures, authored expected rows, SQL and DataFrame starters, solutions and tests. Local Spark 4.0.4, no cloud.

title: Join cardinality and weighted metrics
summary: A plausible incorrect total from a multiplying join, its diagnosis by counts and duplicate keys, the repair, a weighted-rate versus average-of-rates trap, a left-join count trap and a transfer test on a different duplicated dimension.
outcome: Detect and repair a multiplying join, compute a weighted metric correctly and read a null-propagating count.
environment: Python 3.12, Apache Spark 4.0.4 (PySpark, local[2], UI off), Java 21.
evidence: 9 tests executed locally with zero skips; hashes in docs/academy/labs/lab-l03-join-cardinality.json.
downloadDescription: Join-cardinality lab: fixtures with duplicated dimension rows, authored expected totals, starters, solutions and tests. Local Spark 4.0.4, no cloud.

title: Plans, shuffles and skew
summary: Read the plans Spark prints for a narrow chain, a grouped sum, a sort-merge and a broadcast join, a window, a salted join and a cached filter over a 240-row synthetic feed, predict each expensive boundary, then compare the prediction with the jobs, stages, tasks and shuffle records Spark actually executed, including adaptive coalescing, a runtime join switch and skew splitting.
outcome: Locate exchanges and stage boundaries in an explained plan, explain why a hot key never splits by repartitioning, show that salting spreads it while keeping totals, and tell a plan change from an answer change.
environment: Python 3.12, Apache Spark 4.0.4 (PySpark, local[2], UI off, four shuffle partitions), Java 21; shuffle records read from Spark's status store. No timings are measured.
evidence: 14 tests executed locally with zero skips; expected values come from a plain-Python derivation that never imports Spark. Hashes and the recorded adaptive build sides are in docs/academy/labs/lab-l04-plans-shuffle.json.
downloadDescription: Execution-evidence lab: seeded skewed and balanced inspection feeds, an independent expected-value derivation, starter and solution evidence functions and tests. Local Spark 4.0.4, no cloud.

title: Delta versions, merges and maintenance on a real table
summary: Move one small open-source Delta table through nine committed versions (a write, an append, a correcting UPDATE, enabling the change data feed, three MERGE statements with different intentions, a schema-evolving append and OPTIMIZE), predict what Delta will report after each, read it back by version, history, detail, change feed and files, and watch four unsafe requests be refused.
outcome: Predict a table's rows at any version, choose the MERGE clauses an incremental or complete delivery needs, keep stale replays out, evolve a schema deliberately and read maintenance from history without deleting data.
environment: Python 3.12, Apache Spark 4.0.4 with open-source delta-spark 4.0.0 (local[2], UI off), Java 21; the first run downloads the Delta jars from Maven Central unless they are already cached. Not Databricks.
evidence: 19 tests executed locally with zero skips; expected rows, history and change-feed entries are hand-derived in DATA.md. Hashes in docs/academy/labs/lab-l05-delta-snapshots.json.
downloadDescription: Delta lab: six hand-written deliveries, hand-derived expected versions, history and change feed, starters, a reference sequence and tests. Local Spark 4.0.4 with open-source Delta 4.0.0; no cloud.

title: Incremental record resolution
summary: Reuse the unchanged Cinderline resolver as a byte-identical reference and apply it to a second plant's raw deliveries: duplicates, late older revisions, valid corrections, conflicting payloads and unkeyed conflicts.
outcome: Predict accepted state, totals, quarantine and the publication decision for changing records, and explain why replay never inflates accepted totals.
environment: Python 3.12 standard library; the reference resolver is pure Python and is hash-checked against the original package.
evidence: 24 tests executed locally with zero skips; fixture and output hashes and the reference SHA-256 are recorded in docs/academy/labs/lab-l06-record-resolution.json.
downloadDescription: Original resolver reference (unchanged, hash-checked) with a second-plant transfer fixture, authored expected states, starters, solutions and tests. Python 3.12, no Spark.

title: Change events into current and history tables
summary: Turn eighteen fictional part change events, delivered in three batches, into the two tables a change-data pipeline publishes: a current table (one row per key) and a history table (one row per version with a validity interval), under a stated source contract and with the cases that break naive designs: a late arrival, an identical redelivery, a repeated state, a tie on the sequence value, a non-integer sequence and a deleted part that returns.
outcome: State the source contract a change-data flow needs, compute SCD type 1 and type 2 tables with window functions in both the DataFrame API and Spark SQL, and read what a declared AUTO CDC flow would do with the same events.
environment: Local Apache Spark 4.0.4 on one machine (local[2], UI off, UTC) with Python 3.12: no Databricks, no Delta Lake, no declarative pipeline, no network call. PySpark 4.0.4 has no pipelines module, which the runner records; the AUTO CDC adaptation is read, not executed.
evidence: 17 tests executed locally with zero skips: both table computations held to rows written by hand for every planted case, recorded in docs/academy/labs/lab-l07-scd.json.
downloadDescription: Change-data lab: eighteen fictional change events in three batches, the source contract, starters, DataFrame and SQL solutions, hand-written expected tables and tests. Runs on local Spark 4.0.4; nothing connects to Databricks.

title: Streaming with event time, a checkpoint and a restart
summary: Run a real Structured Streaming query over five synthetic press-line files: a 10-minute windowed aggregation with a 5-minute watermark, late rows inside and outside the watermark, a checkpoint that records what each micro-batch planned and committed, a restart that neither loses nor duplicates windows, and foreachBatch delivery to two stand-in downstream systems made idempotent.
outcome: Predict which windows a watermark finalizes and which late rows it drops, read a checkpoint's offsets and commits, and explain why a restart is safe only when the sink write is idempotent.
environment: Python 3.12, Apache Spark 4.0.4 Structured Streaming (PySpark, local[2], trigger availableNow, no sleeps), Java 21; stand-in sinks append to local lists.
evidence: 13 tests executed locally with zero skips; batch results are also re-derived by a plain-Python script that never imports Spark. Hashes in docs/academy/labs/lab-l08-streaming-restart.json.
downloadDescription: Streaming lab: five synthetic landing files with deliberate late rows, hand-derived and independently derived expected windows, starters, a reference query with checkpoint and restart, and tests. Local Spark 4.0.4, no cloud.

title: Failure and recovery boundaries in a four-task pipeline
summary: Break a fictional four-task daily report pipeline (retain the export, resolve lots, publish the report, notify two recipients) at four injected points and recover by re-running the same run id: succeeded tasks are reused, the failed task and its successors run again, and an idempotency key keeps a notification from going out twice. A stale input that turns every task green is refused by a freshness check.
outcome: Explain why a green task is a statement about its own success condition, not about the business data, and design keys, a ledger and a freshness check so a retry or a backfill can never duplicate an effect or move the current report.
environment: Python 3.12 standard library on one machine: no scheduler service, no Lakeflow Jobs run, no Databricks workspace and no network. Failures are injected by raising an exception at a named point; the only external effect appends to a Python list, and no message is ever sent.
evidence: 43 tests executed locally with zero skips; the filled starter passes 41 of 41 in starter mode and the package's mutation check catches 14 of 14 deliberate defects. Recorded in docs/academy/labs/lab-l09-failure-recovery.json.
downloadDescription: Failure-recovery lab: a fictional four-task pipeline with a local runner and ledger, injected failure points, starters, solutions, expected outcomes, tests and a mutation check. Python 3.12 standard library; nothing connects to Databricks or sends a message.

title: Data contracts and quarantine
summary: Validate schema, keys, quantities and cross-record constraints over synthetic inspection deliveries, quarantine rows with reasons, and show why row-level checks cannot establish uniqueness or completeness on their own.
outcome: Write a contract-driven validator, read a quarantine by reason, and separate row-level validity from multi-row and source-completeness evidence.
environment: Python 3.12 standard library.
evidence: 19 tests executed locally with zero skips, including a permissive validator that fails for the asserted reason; hashes in docs/academy/labs/lab-l10-contracts-quarantine.json.
downloadDescription: Contract validator lab: fixtures, expected quarantine with reasons, manifest-count transfer case, starters, solutions and tests. Python 3.12, no Spark.

title: Model it, then contract the metric
summary: Build a small star schema from synthetic accepted inspections (one fact at the grain of one inspection; line, plant, shift and date dimensions; supervisor history as type 2 rows), compute a unit defect rate at line-day, plant-day and plant-month from a metric contract, then watch five deliberately broken queries fail for their stated reasons.
outcome: Declare a fact's grain, keep type 2 history joinable at a point in time, compute a ratio metric from summed numerator and denominator at any level, and recognize averaging of rates, many-to-many double counts and calendar-window mismatches.
environment: Python 3.12, Apache Spark 4.0.4 (PySpark, local[2], UI off, session time zone UTC), Java 21; no Unity Catalog object or metric view.
evidence: 20 tests executed locally with zero skips; running them with --sql starters/model.sql against the unfilled starter shows most fail until the gaps are filled. Hashes in docs/academy/labs/lab-l11-modeling-metrics.json.
downloadDescription: Modeling and metrics lab: synthetic inspections and dimensions, a metric contract, hand-derived expected results, a starter and a reference star schema with SQL, and tests. Local Spark 4.0.4, no cloud.

title: Time-aware analytical SQL
summary: A Spark SQL portfolio over five synthetic plant files: window frames, ranking and deduplication, gaps and islands, membership with EXISTS versus IN and NULLs, set operations, nested fields, safe casts under ANSI mode and daylight-saving-time arithmetic, with every expected value written down before the query ran.
outcome: Predict a window's rows and a query's result row by row, choose the membership form that survives NULLs, cast defensively, and state which time zone a timestamp calculation used.
environment: Python 3.12, Apache Spark 4.0.4 (PySpark, local[2], UI off, ANSI mode on, session time zone America/New_York), Java 21.
evidence: 51 tests executed locally with zero skips; time-zone answers come from an independent zoneinfo script that never touches Spark. Hashes in docs/academy/labs/lab-l12-time-aware-sql.json.
downloadDescription: Analytical SQL lab: five synthetic fixtures, hand-derived and independently derived expected results, a starter and a reference SQL portfolio, and tests. Local Spark 4.0.4, no cloud.

title: A reproducible cost worksheet and a controlled cost experiment
summary: Build a cost worksheet a reader can recompute: six cost drivers in their own units and periods with explicitly hypothetical rates, restated per month in one currency across low, base and high cases, the one-off migration kept apart and the most sensitive input named; then turn synthetic run observations into cost per unit of work and refuse the rows that cannot honestly be divided.
outcome: Keep units, periods and currency explicit, compare only comparable alternatives, find the input that moves the answer most, and compute cost per unit of work with named refusals instead of guesses.
environment: Python 3.12 standard library only; every rate is a labelled hypothetical rate, not a price.
evidence: 30 tests executed locally with zero skips; expected values are derived independently in DATA.md. Hashes in docs/academy/labs/lab-l13-cost-model.json.
downloadDescription: Cost-model lab: hypothetical rates and workload inputs, synthetic run observations, independently derived expected results, starters, a reference worksheet and tests. Python 3.12 standard library; no live prices.

title: Governance review: access decisions, filters and masks
summary: A tabletop review of a fictional principal, object and action matrix: predict who may do what and which check decides (USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA before SELECT, deny by default, ownership, inherited privileges), what a row filter and a column mask return for each caller, and which negative cases a review must test; a small local evaluator checks the answers against hand-written keys.
outcome: Read an access table the way Unity Catalog evaluates it, predict filtered and masked results per caller, and design the negative tests an access review needs.
environment: Worked on paper or in an editor; answers are checked by a Python 3.12 standard-library evaluator. A locally evaluated policy table is not Unity Catalog enforcement: no GRANT, filter, mask, ABAC policy, authentication or audit query was executed.
evidence: 23 tests executed locally with zero skips against hand-written answer keys; the seven platform steps that were not executed are listed in docs/academy/labs/lab-l14-governance-review.json.
downloadDescription: Governance tabletop: a fictional access matrix, filter and mask policies, callers, answer templates, hand-written keys, a local evaluator and tests. Python 3.12 standard library; nothing connects to Databricks.

title: Three-cloud request-path diagnosis
summary: A tabletop diagnosis of one refused and one unreachable request on each of AWS, Azure and Google Cloud, built from the three cloud modules' own worked examples: follow the query through its author, control, execution and storage paths as text tables, name the control that decided, and choose the evidence that proves it before changing anything. A small local evaluator checks the answers against keys written by hand.
outcome: Diagnose a denied and an unreachable request in the same order on any of the three clouds, separating identity and authorization from network reachability, and name the evidence that would confirm each hypothesis.
environment: Worked on paper or in an editor; answers are checked by a Python 3.12 standard-library evaluator. Nothing resolves a name, sends a packet, reads a policy or contacts AWS, Azure, Google Cloud or Databricks; hostnames and account identifiers are synthetic placeholders.
evidence: 30 evaluator tests executed locally with zero skips against hand-written keys; the eight platform steps that were not executed are listed in docs/academy/labs/lab-l15-three-cloud-diagnosis.json.
downloadDescription: Three-cloud tabletop: a case sheet per cloud with request paths, identities, controls and an evidence catalogue, answer templates, hand-written keys, a local evaluator and tests. Python 3.12 standard library; nothing connects to a cloud or to Databricks.

title: Deliver a job as a reviewed package and bundle
summary: Turn a fictional daily scrap-rate job, once a hand-copied notebook with a pasted token, into a small Python package with its own unit tests and a Declarative Automation Bundle (formerly Databricks Asset Bundles) with dev, test and prod targets. Local checks parse the bundle, apply 21 structure rules, resolve each target's configuration and run the package tests; every Databricks step is named and left not run.
outcome: Explain what each delivery state proves (local source, validation, reviewed artifact, deployment, execution), keep environment differences in configuration, and read a bundle's targets the way validate and deploy would.
environment: Python 3.12 with PyYAML 6.0.3 on one machine. The Databricks CLI and SDK are not installed, no workspace is contacted and no token exists; the test runner refuses network connections and subprocesses.
evidence: 16 local tests executed with zero skips (including the package's 14 unit tests), recorded in docs/academy/labs/lab-l16-bundle-delivery.json. Authentication, bundle validate, plan, deploy, run, integration tests and promotion are listed as NOT RUN.
downloadDescription: Delivery lab: a small Python package with unit tests, the bundle configuration as fenced files in BUNDLE.md, fixtures, a local bundle checker, expected outputs and a promotion checklist. Python 3.12 and PyYAML; nothing connects to Databricks.

title: A baseline, a tracked experiment and an evidence-based promotion
summary: Predict a coating-oven fault stop from a small seeded synthetic dataset: a naive baseline and a simple model, a leaking split exposed and corrected by time, comparable runs tracked in open-source MLflow with parameters, metrics, dataset digests and signatures, an impressive run that cannot be reproduced, a model contract that refuses schema drift and a promotion decision that reads the evidence before the metrics.
outcome: Compare a model with a baseline under a time-based split, record runs so a result can be rerun exactly, enforce a model's input contract and justify or refuse a promotion from its evidence.
environment: Python 3.12 with MLflow 3.16.1, scikit-learn 1.9.1, pandas 3.0.6, numpy 2.5.3, scipy 1.18.1 and skops 0.15.0; MLflow tracks into a file store in a temporary directory; no tracking server, Unity Catalog or network.
evidence: 32 tests executed locally with zero skips; expected metrics come from an independent derivation script, and the temporary tracking store is deleted. Hashes in docs/academy/labs/lab-l17-baseline-mlflow.json.
downloadDescription: Tracked-experiment lab: a seeded oven-day generator and fixture, a data dictionary, independently derived expected metrics, starters, a reference solution and tests. Open-source MLflow with a local file store; no Databricks.

title: Point-in-time features
summary: Build a feature table from timestamped sensor readings whose two-hour windows publish thirty minutes after they close, join it to labelled prediction times as of what was actually known, and prove that future readings, duplicate entity-time rows and a drifted serving transform are all rejected.
outcome: Construct a point-in-time-correct training set, name the leak in event-time and latest-value shortcuts, catch training/serving skew with a consistency check, and explain which predictions change when late readings append new feature versions.
environment: Python 3.12 with pandas 3.0.6 and numpy 2.5.3; no Spark, Java, MLflow or network.
evidence: 25 tests executed locally with zero skips, including shortcut starters that fail for their documented reason; hashes in docs/academy/labs/lab-l18-point-in-time-features.json.
downloadDescription: Point-in-time feature lab: timestamped readings, late arrivals, labels, a feature contract, authored expected tables, starters with deliberate shortcuts, a reference solution and tests. Python 3.12 with pandas; no Spark.

title: Forecasts, anomaly thresholds and a ranked queue
summary: Three decisions on a fictional production line that each get called prediction and each need their own evaluation: a weekly unit forecast judged by rolling-origin backtests against naive and seasonal baselines, an anomaly score for daily defect counts with a threshold table that prices every flag, and a ranked inspection queue judged by precision at k.
outcome: Choose the horizon, the baseline and the backtest before the model; read an interval and an anomaly threshold as costs; and rank a queue by the metric the shift can act on.
environment: pandas 3.0.6, numpy 2.5.3 and scikit-learn 1.9.1 on Python 3.12, one machine, CPU only, no network: no Spark, no Databricks, no AutoML and no model service.
evidence: 41 tests executed locally with zero skips against literals derived independently in the standard library, including the fixture checked byte for byte and six deliberate shortcuts shown to fail, recorded in docs/academy/labs/lab-l19-forecast-anomaly.json.
downloadDescription: Forecasting lab: a seeded daily fixture, starters with six deliberate shortcuts, solutions, an independent expected-value derivation and tests. pandas, numpy and scikit-learn on one machine; nothing connects to Databricks.

title: Retrieval quality on a governed lexical baseline
summary: Build a small TF-IDF retriever over eighteen fictional maintenance documents with version, effective date, plant and audience metadata. Compare two chunk sizes, filter by permission before ranking, prefer current revisions, measure recall@k and MRR on labelled questions, and watch the wrong chunk win, a newer authorized source change the answer and an unauthorized document stay out.
outcome: Evaluate retrieval separately from answer quality, place the permission filter before ranking, handle superseded and region-restricted documents, and explain why a lexical baseline fails where it does.
environment: Python 3.12 with scikit-learn 1.9.1 (TfidfVectorizer), numpy and scipy; lexical retrieval only: no neural embeddings, no vector index, no Databricks AI Search, no network.
evidence: 28 tests executed locally with zero skips; expected relevant chunks are authored per question. Hashes in docs/academy/labs/lab-l20-retrieval-quality.json.
downloadDescription: Retrieval lab: eighteen fictional documents with metadata, labelled questions with expected chunks, starters, a reference retriever and evaluator, and tests. scikit-learn TF-IDF; no embeddings or managed service.

title: Evaluation harness, traces and a failure taxonomy
summary: Build a deterministic evaluation harness for a fictional read-only maintenance assistant: twelve cases with expected properties written before any answer exists, six scorers for citations, abstention, forbidden tools and required fields, a classifier that reads each trace span by span and names the failure (retrieval, reasoning, denied tool, policy block), and a deliberately lenient citation scorer rejected against reference verdicts.
outcome: State expected properties before evaluating, score them deterministically, locate a failure in a trace, validate a scorer before trusting it, and reuse the harness on a second domain.
environment: Python 3.12 standard library only; answers and traces are authored fixtures, not model outputs, and no model, hosted judge or endpoint is called.
evidence: 33 tests executed locally with zero skips, including a lenient scorer that fails for its asserted reason. Hashes in docs/academy/labs/lab-l21-evaluation-traces.json.
downloadDescription: Evaluation lab: sources, tools, cases with expected properties, authored answer and trace fixtures, reference verdicts, starters, reference scorers and classifier, and tests. Python 3.12 standard library; no model calls.

title: Tool calls behind an application-side policy gate
summary: Build the policy gate between a fictional maintenance assistant and three local stand-ins for real systems. It decides each scripted tool proposal from the signed-in user's session, the exposed tools and their schemas, the user's grants intersected with the application's delegated scopes, an idempotency key and an approval policy, and writes one audit row per decision. Twenty scripted proposals and five approval actions, some carrying instructions injected into retrieved documents, attack it.
outcome: Explain why a model's proposal is not an authorization, and implement and test the checks an application makes before a tool call has any effect: identity, schema, delegated permission, idempotent retries, human approval and audit.
environment: Python 3.12 standard library on one machine: no packages, no network, no language model, no MCP server and no Databricks workspace. Scripted proposals stand in for a model, and every effect is an append to an in-memory list.
evidence: 41 tests executed locally with zero skips against hand-written expected decisions, effects and audit rows; the package's mutation check catches all nine deliberate gate defects. Recorded in docs/academy/labs/lab-l22-tool-authorization.json.
downloadDescription: Policy-gate lab: fictional sessions, grants, tools, documents with injected instructions and scripted proposals, starters, solutions, expected decisions and audit rows, tests and a mutation check. Python 3.12 standard library; nothing connects to a model, an MCP server or Databricks.

title: Transactional state for a quality-review app
summary: Constraints, an idempotent at-least-once intake, a work queue claimed with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED across two real sessions, optimistic concurrency with a version column, isolation timelines and a least-privilege application role, all on a local PostgreSQL 16 server, plus a Lakebase adaptation guide kept separate from what ran.
outcome: Design operational state that survives redelivery and concurrent reviewers, show why an unlocked read-then-update double-claims and last-write-wins loses a decision, and list what a managed Lakebase deployment would still need to prove.
environment: Python 3.12 standard library driving a throwaway local PostgreSQL 16 server (initdb, pg_ctl, psql) on 127.0.0.1; managed Lakebase, OAuth, the pooler and synced tables were not executed.
evidence: 18 tests executed locally against PostgreSQL 16.13 with zero skips; ten Lakebase platform steps are listed as not executed in docs/academy/labs/lab-l23-transactional-state.json.
downloadDescription: Transactional-state lab: schema, grants, claim, decision and intake SQL with starters, fixtures, hand-derived expected results, a local PostgreSQL 16 test harness and a Lakebase adaptation guide. Requires PostgreSQL 16 server tools; no Databricks workspace.

title: Migrate a nightly job and reconcile it row by row
summary: Translate a fictional SQL Server stored procedure and SSIS-style package into Spark SQL job tasks and prove, row by row against hand-authored legacy outputs, where the translation keeps or changes meaning: collation and trailing spaces, predicates in a LEFT JOIN's ON clause, the business-day clock, integer division, exact money, watermarks and a parallel-run cutover gate.
outcome: Inventory legacy logic before translating, reproduce legacy meaning with explicit choices, reconcile keyed differences, totals and NULLs, and decide a cutover from parallel-run evidence rather than from row counts.
environment: Python 3.12, Apache Spark 4.0.4 (PySpark, local[2], UI off), Java 21; no SQL Server, SSIS or Agent instance, and no Databricks workspace.
evidence: 28 tests executed locally with zero skips; the legacy outputs are hand-authored fixtures derived in DATA.md. Hashes in docs/academy/labs/lab-l24-migration-reconciliation.json.
downloadDescription: Migration and reconciliation lab: the legacy procedure and package outline as text, legacy-output fixtures, a transfer plant, parallel-run scenarios, starters, a reference translation and tests. Local Spark 4.0.4, no SQL Server or cloud.
